div.head: Relations
div.p: A relation is a typed statement from one thing to another: a chapter is a text of a council's canon, a manuscript was owned by an abbey, a hand was a scribe's, a bishop held office in a church. It joins records, nodes of texts, or other relations, and may carry a date, a certainty, a role and a place, its evidence, its author, and, for a judgement, its method. Facts that belong to one record alone are its fields (); what joins two things, may be uncertain or disputed, or needs evidence, is a relation.

A file writes its relations in the standOff's listRelation, one relation each. The import reads them as the encoder's statements, beside the observations it makes itself from the source notes () and the relations it makes from a description's history (). Relations are full.

div.head: The form of a relation

list.item: its type: name, the type's name (isTextOf), and, in exports, ref, the type's permalink;
observation or judgement: type, observation for what a witness shows, judgement for what holds of a version or a work, naming its evidence;
its author: resp, pointing to the person who states it;
its date, where the type has one (an owner's years, an office's), in the relation's own attributes, in the one form ();
its evidence: the passages it rests on, by pointers in source, and the publications, with their pages, in its description.

div.p: TEI 4.12 lets a relation hold one desc, and nothing else. What the type needs beyond its ends goes there, each in its element:

list.item: a role (bishop, abbot, owner), by roleName;
a place (an office held in a diocese), by placeName with ref;
a judgement's method ("in all witnesses", "in the canonical witness", "the editor's text", "the register"), by term typed method;
what a text came through, for derivedFrom, by ptr typed via, pointing to the work, version or transcription;
a publication as evidence, by a bibl holding a ptr to it and its pages in citedRange.

div.head: The types
div.p: Each type says what it joins, and has a reverse: "a version of" reads back as "has as a version". The six types of the texts' levels and units are fixed; the others are a vocabulary of the application, which grows as the project needs, each type mapped later to SAWS or another ontology. The guide holds the types to start with; a name outside them is reported, so that a slip is seen and a new type is added to the vocabulary on purpose.

div.p: A family of texts is never encoded: the application works it out from the relations.

constraintSpec.desc: A relation's type is one of the types to start with, or a new term of the vocabulary.

sch:rule.sch:assert: The relation type isn't among the guide's types: check its spelling, or add it to the application's vocabulary.

div.head: The levels' relations
div.p: The four relations between the levels, versionOf, witnessOf, transcriptionOf and in, are the ones an imported file needs least: the import makes them from the header. A file's text is a transcription of its witness; the witness is in the manuscript or the publication its source description gives (), at its folios or pages, and is a witness of the work its code names. An encoder writes them only to say more: that a version listed in the file is a version of a work, or that a witness is of a version and not only of its work. An export writes the levels' ids in the formal title (), and their relations in its standOff.

isTextOf joins a node of a witness to its version's canon: it is how a witness's own structure is mapped to the canons (). The import makes it as an observation from each source note that names a canon; an encoder writes it where no note does.
